first_delegated.default_label: 11:00 (Longstreet 1896 memoir; OR bound before about noon)

basis.text: Longstreet's article of 1877 ('fully eleven o'clock when General Lee ... ordered the movement') and his book of 1896 ('It was eleven o'clock when General Lee's order was issued'), repeated by Alexander (1907), bounded by Longstreet's report of 27 July 1863 and Kershaw's of 1 October 1863 (instructions before about noon; Kershaw directed to move about noon). No report of the time gives an hour.

default.label: About 11:00: Lee's order to Longstreet to attack the enemy's left (Longstreet's hour); before about noon

animation.note: 11:00 is the best-supported instant for the formal order and is the plan's own time; it is later than the early-morning plan (Fremantle, 7 a.m.) and earlier than the march (about noon), so it is not earlier than any source-supported time of the order. It drives no unit, arrival or gate; the plan to attack the left is shown as known in the morning and the earlier values stay selectable.

default.note: Longstreet is the only source of the hour and wrote 14 and 33 years later; 'fully eleven' leaves room for a little after eleven. The reports of the time bound it before about noon.

positions.label: About 11:00: Lee's order to Longstreet (the plan's value and its recommended default; Longstreet's own hour)

value.note: 'fully eleven o'clock' (1877) and 'eleven o'clock' (1896): eleven or a little after, and before about noon

support.page_note: Longstreet, 'The Campaign of Gettysburg', first printed in the Philadelphia Weekly Times in 1877 and reprinted in The Annals of the War (1879) p. 422; the page head 422 stands before the passage and the head 423 after it. Hoke (1887) and the Southern Historical Society Papers vol. 5 print the same sentence.
support.quote: It was fully eleven o'clock when General Lee arrived at this conclusion and ordered the movement

witness.name: James Longstreet
witness.role: Lieutenant General commanding the First Corps

support.note: Longstreet received the order, so he writes as the man it was given to. 'Fully' keeps the hour as a lower bound (eleven or a little after). The same paragraph has Lee back from Ewell's lines 'at about nine o'clock' and 'about forty minutes' of waiting for Law's brigade.

support.page_note: From Manassas to Appomattox (1896), chapter on the second day at Gettysburg, p. 365 (running heads 365 and 366 read in the text layer).
support.quote: It was eleven o'clock when General Lee's order was issued, but he had ordered Law's brigade to its division

witness.name: James Longstreet
witness.role: Lieutenant General commanding the First Corps

support.note: The book repeats and shortens the article of 1877 (the same writer and the same story, 33 years after the day).

support.page_note: From Manassas to Appomattox (1896) p. 382 (head 382 before the passage, head 383 after). Taylor, General Lee (1906) prints the same sentence while answering it.
support.quote: Not one word did he utter to me of their march until he gave his orders at eleven o'clock for the move to his right

witness.name: James Longstreet
witness.role: Lieutenant General commanding the First Corps

phrases: gave his orders at eleven o'clock

support.note: Longstreet answering Walter Taylor's statement that Lee was impatient for the First Corps: Lee said nothing to him of the march until the orders of eleven o'clock.

support.page_note: Military Memoirs of a Confederate (1907), chapter 'Gettysburg: Second Day', p. 391 (head 391 before the passage, head 392 after). The text layer prints 'About 11 A.M.'; the same page prints 'Lee's order at 11 A.M.' a page later.
support.quote: About 11 A.M., his orders were issued

witness.name: E. Porter Alexander
witness.role: Colonel, commanding the reserve artillery battalion of the First Corps (later chief of the corps artillery)

support.note: Alexander reached the field at 9 a.m. and was not at Lee's headquarters; he does not say how he knew the hour. His sequence (Lee to the left about nine, back about ten, orders about eleven) is the sequence of Longstreet's book (Freeman, Lee vol. 3 note, reads Longstreet's book as 'It was 10 o'clock when Lee returned'), so it is counted with Longstreet's line of knowledge.

inference.step: The day is the 2 July of each chapter. Longstreet, who received the order, put it at 'fully eleven o'clock' in 1877 and at eleven in 1896; Alexander's book follows the same sequence; Longstreet's report of 1863 and Kershaw's report put the instructions before Law's brigade joined about noon and the march order about noon, which an order at about eleven fits; so about 11:00 is the best-supported hour, stated by one line of knowledge.

positions.label: Not later than about noon: Lee's instructions had reached Longstreet before Law's brigade joined

value.note: an upper bound ('previous to his joining', Law joined about noon), not an hour

support.quote: joined about noon on the 2d. Previous to his joining, I received instructions from the commanding general to move

witness.name: James Longstreet
witness.role: Lieutenant General commanding the First Corps

phrases: Previous to his joining, I received instructions from the commanding general to move

support.note: Longstreet's report of 27 July 1863 (25 days after the day). It gives no hour for the instructions; it says only that they came before Law's brigade joined, about noon. It says nothing against 11:00.

support.quote: halted until about noon. We were then directed to move under cover of the hills toward the right

witness.name: Joseph B. Kershaw
witness.role: Brigadier General commanding the South Carolina brigade of McLaws's division

phrases: We were then directed to move under cover of the hills toward the right

support.note: Kershaw's brigade was halted 'until about noon' and then directed to move. That is the march order reaching a brigade, which follows Lee's order to Longstreet and the wait for Law; it does not date Lee's order.

support.quote: about midday General Longstreet arrived and viewed the ground

witness.name: William N. Pendleton
witness.role: Brigadier General, chief of artillery of the Army of Northern Virginia

phrases: about midday General Longstreet arrived and viewed the ground

support.note: Pendleton's report of 12 September 1863. Longstreet was at the forward ground on the right about midday: the order to him had been given by then. Pendleton also says that after sunrise he understood the commanding general's purpose to be an attack on the enemy's left (see the early-plan position).

reason_not_chosen.text: This is the ceiling the reports of 1863 give, not an hour: the order was given before about noon. 11:00 satisfies it, so it limits the default and does not replace it.

inference.step: The day is 2 July in each report. Longstreet's report says Law joined about noon and that his instructions came previously; Kershaw's brigade was halted until about noon and then directed to move; Pendleton has Longstreet at the forward ground about midday; so the order was given before about noon.

positions.label: Early morning: the plan to attack the enemy's left already known in the First Corps before the formal order

support.page_note: Diary entry for 2 July 1863 in the transcription of the Edinburgh edition of 1863 (no page numbers); the same entry is on p. 257 of the American edition of 1864.
support.quote: At 7 A.M. I rode over part of the ground with General Longstreet, and saw him disposing M'Laws's division for to-day's fight

witness.name: Arthur J. L. Fremantle
witness.role: Lieutenant Colonel, Coldstream Guards, British observer with Longstreet's staff

support.note: The diary of the day: at 7 a.m. Longstreet was placing McLaws's division 'for to-day's fight'. It does not say that Lee's order had been given.

support.page_note: Same entry, a few paragraphs later; no page numbers in this transcription (p. 257 of the American edition of 1864).
support.quote: As the whole morning was evidently to be occupied in disposing the troops for the attack

witness.name: Arthur J. L. Fremantle
witness.role: Lieutenant Colonel, Coldstream Guards, British observer with Longstreet's staff

phrases: disposing the troops for the attack

support.note: The diarist's own reading of the morning: the troops were being disposed for an attack, which he took to occupy the whole forenoon.

support.quote: I received a communication from the commanding general, the tenor of which was that he intended the main attack to be made by the First Corps

witness.name: Richard S. Ewell
witness.role: Lieutenant General commanding the Second Corps

phrases: the main attack to be made by the First Corps

support.note: Ewell's report; the sentence before it begins 'Early in the morning'. He gives no hour, and the dateline of the report prints only '1863' (the month is blank in the scan); it is read here only for the order of events (a message of Lee's about the main attack came to Ewell in the morning), not as a clock.

support.quote: Shortly after our arrival, I was directed by General Longstreet to accompany with my battalion the divisions of Major-Generals McLaws and Hood in the attack upon the left

witness.name: E. Porter Alexander
witness.role: Colonel, commanding the reserve artillery battalion of the First Corps

phrases: in the attack upon the left

support.note: Alexander's report of 3 August 1863. The arrival is 'at 9 a. m. on July 2' (the sentence before). 'Shortly after' is not a clock, and the order named is Longstreet's to Alexander, not Lee's to Longstreet; the report was written 32 days later and may compress the morning.

support.page_note: McLaws, 'The Battle of Gettysburg', address of 1879, Southern Historical Society Papers vol. 7 pp. 67-69; the quoted words are on p. 68 (heads 67 and 68 read in the text layer).
support.quote: General, I wish you to place your division across this road

phrases: I wish you to place your division across this road

support.note: McLaws says that soon after his division reached the hill, early in the morning, Lee himself told him where to place it. No hour. A memory of 1879 about the morning.

reason_not_chosen.text: These show the plan and the first dispositions in the morning, before the formal order to move; none gives an hour for Lee's order, and Longstreet places that order later, about eleven.

inference.step: The day is 2 July (the diary entry's date; the reports' own days). A diary of the day has Longstreet disposing McLaws's division at 7 a.m. 'for to-day's fight'; Ewell was told in the morning that the main attack was the First Corps's; Alexander was directed 'shortly after' his 9 a.m. arrival to go with the divisions 'in the attack upon the left'; McLaws says Lee himself told him where to place his division soon after he arrived; so the intent to attack on the right was in the corps's hands in the morning, though not dated by any clock as an order.

positions.label: About 09:00: Lee back from Ewell's lines (not the order)

value.note: Longstreet: Lee 'returned at about nine o'clock'; Freeman and Alexander place the trip later or differently

support.page_note: Same article and page as the 'fully eleven' sentence.
support.quote: He returned at about nine o'clock, and informed me that it would not do to have Ewell open the attack

witness.name: James Longstreet
witness.role: Lieutenant General commanding the First Corps

phrases: He returned at about nine o'clock

support.note: 'He' is Lee, back from Ewell's lines. Longstreet gives about nine for the return and about eleven for the order. Freeman calls the nine 'an impossibility'.

support.page_note: R. E. Lee vol. 3, p. 92, a footnote answering Longstreet's chronology (head 92 before the passage, head 93 after).
support.quote: there are abundant witnesses that Lee was at Ewell's headquarters about 9 A.M

witness.name: Douglas Southall Freeman
witness.role: historian, biographer of Lee (not a participant)

support.note: Freeman puts Lee at Ewell's headquarters at about nine, so the return was later (he says the incidents before the return 'could hardly have consumed less than two hours'). He does not name the witnesses in the passage cited here.

support.page_note: Military Memoirs of a Confederate (1907) p. 391, the paragraph before 'About 11 A.M., his orders were issued'.
support.quote: About nine o'clock, he rode to the left and conferred again with Ewell and Early

witness.name: E. Porter Alexander
witness.role: Colonel, commanding the reserve artillery battalion of the First Corps (later chief of the corps artillery)

phrases: he rode to the left and conferred again with Ewell and Early

support.note: Alexander has Lee riding to the left at nine and back at ten, which differs from Longstreet (left after sunrise, back about nine). The two accounts of the same trip disagree by an hour or more.

reason_not_chosen.text: Nine o'clock is where the sources put Lee's visit to Ewell's lines or his return; Longstreet says the order came about two hours after it. The accounts of the trip itself disagree.

inference.step: The day is 2 July in each source. Longstreet says the return from Ewell's lines was about nine and the order about eleven; Freeman has Lee still at Ewell's headquarters about nine; Alexander has him riding left at nine and back at ten; so a nine o'clock event exists in the record, and it is Lee's trip, not the order.

positions.label: About 15:00: decision to go on without Pickett (Hood's memory)

support.page_note: Hood's letter to Longstreet of 28 June 1875, printed in Advance and Retreat (1880) pp. 55-58; the sentence is on p. 57 (head 57 before it, head 58 after the following paragraph).
support.quote: in the afternoon about 3 o'clock it was decided to no longer await Pickett's Division

phrases: it was decided to no longer await Pickett's Division

support.note: Hood, writing 'from memory', has Lee anxious for an attack in the morning, Longstreet wishing to wait for Pickett, and the decision to go on without him at about 3 in the afternoon. The march began about noon (Kershaw; Longstreet's report), so the 3 o'clock is not the order.

reason_not_chosen.text: Hood wrote from memory in 1875. Longstreet's report and Kershaw's report of 1863 have the instructions before about noon and the march ordered about noon, hours before 3 p.m.

inference.step: The day is 2 July (Hood's letter). Hood says that about 3 in the afternoon it was decided to go forward without Pickett; the reports of 1863 have the march ordered about noon, so Hood's hour dates his own advance or a later decision, not Lee's order.

weighing.summary: One line of knowledge gives an hour: Longstreet, who received the order, wrote 'fully eleven o'clock' in 1877 and 'eleven o'clock' in 1896; Alexander's book (1907) and Hoke (1887) repeat it. No report of 1863 gives an hour; the reports only bound the order before about noon (Longstreet's report: instructions before Law's brigade joined about noon; Kershaw: directed to move about noon). The other value, 09:00, has no source found: it is a forum's figure, and nine o'clock is where Longstreet puts Lee's return from Ewell's lines. The plan to attack the left was already known in the corps in the morning (Fremantle at 7, Alexander's report, McLaws), so 'order' means the formal order to move.
weighing.who: Longstreet received the order and was the corps commander, so he stands where the order landed; Alexander was a colonel who arrived at nine and was not at Lee's headquarters; Kershaw, Pendleton and Ewell wrote reports of 1863 as officers present. Lee's own report gives the assignments and no hour. Taylor, Marshall, Long and Venable wrote in 1875 and say only that they never heard of a sunrise order.
weighing.when: Longstreet's report of 27 July 1863 (25 days) and Alexander's of 3 August 1863 (rank 5), Pendleton's of 12 September (rank 4) and Kershaw's of 1 October (91 days, rank 4) outrank the memoirs; but none states an hour for the order. The hour comes from reminiscence of 14 years (1877, rank 2) and 33 years (1896), and from Alexander's book of 1907 (rank 2).
weighing.where: Longstreet was with Lee and received the order; the reports of the time that bound it were written on the spot. Hood was with his division, not at headquarters, and his 3 p.m. is his decision about the march. Fremantle was with Longstreet from 7 a.m. and describes dispositions, not an order.
weighing.how_knew: Longstreet knew by being given the order, and says in the same paragraph that Lee came back from Ewell about nine and that he waited about forty minutes for Law. Alexander does not say how he knew the hour; his sequence follows Longstreet's. The reports of 1863 give the bounds from the writers' own movements.
weighing.clock: Longstreet, Alexander, Kershaw, Pendleton and Ewell wrote on the Confederate clock. Fremantle's watch is not named. The reported difference of about 20 minutes between the two armies' clocks is not applied; it is small beside the two hours between the plan's two values and cannot move 11:00 to 09:00.
weighing.independence: Groups: longstreet (his article of 1877, his book of 1896 and Alexander's book, whose sequence of the morning is Longstreet's); longstreet-report-1863; kershaw; pendleton; ewell; alexander-report-1863; fremantle; mclaws-1879; freeman; hood-letter-1875. The hour 11:00 therefore rests on one group and carries the flags single_source and memoir_only. The bound 'before about noon' rests on three groups of reports of the time.
weighing.overrides: A rejected value outranks the default by class only where it is a report of the time: Alexander's report ('shortly after' his 9 a.m. arrival) and Ewell's ('early in the morning') are better classed than Longstreet's memoirs, but they date Longstreet's order to Alexander and a message to Ewell, not Lee's order to Longstreet; they are carried as the early-plan value and do not contradict the formal order at about eleven. The 09:00 of the plan has no document at all.

source_panel_text: About 11:00 on Jul 2: Longstreet, who received Lee's order, wrote in 1877 'fully eleven o'clock' and in 1896 eleven; his 1863 report only puts it before about noon. No report of the time gives an hour. The plan's 09:00 rests on a forum and has no source found; nine o'clock is when Lee came back from Ewell. Five other values are listed.

what_would_change_it: A report, letter, diary or dispatch of 2 July 1863 that gives the hour of Lee's order to Longstreet (a staff diary, Lee's or Longstreet's headquarters log, a dispatch to Ewell or Hill timing the order, Johnston's own account, or a regimental diary of the First Corps), or a page of the Civil War Talk thread and the Epperson timeline that names a primary source for 09:00 or 11:00. A witness with Lee at headquarters that morning (Taylor, Marshall, Venable, Long) stating the hour would also settle it.
